claims.source: Tenomodulin, a type II transmembrane glycoprotein, is expressed in tendons and ligaments and is a regulator of tenocyte proliferation and is involved in collagen fibril maturation (Docheva et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Docheva et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Mohawk, EGR1, and EGR2 are transcription factors involved in tendon formation.
claims.source: Further studies have shown that Mohawk (Liu et al., 2010), EGR1, and EGR2 are transcription factors that are also involved in tendon formation (Lejard et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2010 and Lejard et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The ability of EGR1 to promote tendon differentiation is partially mediated by TGFβ2.
claims.source: Furthermore, the ability of EGR1 to promote tendon differentiation is partially mediated by TGFβ2 (Guerquin et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Guerquin et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Two main signalling pathways, TGFβ and FGF, have been identified in vertebrate tendon development.
claims.source: Two main signalling pathways, TGFβ and FGF, have been identified in vertebrate tendon development (Maeda et al., 2011, and for review see Tozer and Duprez, 2005; Schweitzer et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Maeda et al., 2011, Tozer and Duprez, 2005, and Schweitzer et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Collagen type I occurs in virtually all fibrous tissues along with type III, V, XII, XIV, fibronectin and small proteoglycans such as decorin.
claims.source: Collagen type I occurs in virtually all fibrous tissues along with type III, V (Birk and Mayne, 1997), XII, XIV (Ansorge et al., 2009), fibronectin and small proteoglycans such as decorin (Berenson et al., 1996; Zhang et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Birk and Mayne, 1997; Ansorge et al., 2009; Berenson et al., 1996; and Zhang et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The defining event that signifies the onset of functional tendon development is the appearance of collagen fibrils in the ECM.
claims.source: The defining event that signifies the onset of functional tendon development is the appearance of collagen fibrils in the ECM.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field of tendon development.

claims.claim: The distribution of collagen fibril diameters distinguishes two stages in tendon development.
claims.source: The distribution of collagen fibril diameters distinguishes two stages in tendon development.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2 showing unimodal distribution in embryonic tendon and bimodal distribution in postnatal tendon.

claims.claim: In mouse, stage 1 begins at E12.5 when narrow (∼35 nm) diameter collagen fibrils are formed within actin-dependent fibripositors at the cell surface.
claims.source: In mouse, stage 1 begins at E12.5 when narrow (∼35 nm) diameter collagen fibrils are formed within actin-dependent fibripositors at the cell surface (Canty et al., 2004, 2006; Kalson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Canty et al., 2004, 2006 and Kalson et al., 2013.

claims.claim: During embryonic tendon development, the length and width of the tissue doubles in a few days, accompanied by two-orders of magnitude increases in elastic modulus and ultimate tensile strength.
claims.source: The length and width of the tissue doubles in a few days, and is accompanied by two-orders of magnitude increases in elastic modulus and ultimate tensile strength (McBride et al., 1985, 1988).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to McBride et al., 1985, 1988.

claims.claim: Serial section transmission electron microscopy of chick embryonic tendon showed that the tendon matrix contains bundles of collagen fibrils that undergo gradual rotation over several microns.
claims.source: Serial section transmission electron microscopy (ss-TEM) of chick embryonic tendon showed that the tendon matrix contains bundles of collagen fibrils that undergo gradual rotation over several microns (Birk and Trelstad, 1986; Birk et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Birk and Trelstad, 1986 and Birk et al., 1989.

claims.claim: The collagen fibril bundles are stabilised by cell–cell connections containing cadherin-11.
claims.source: Moreover, the collagen fibril bundles are stabilised by cell–cell connections containing cadherin-11 (Richardson et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Richardson et al., 2007.

claims.claim: During stage 1 there is a modest increase in fibril diameter (to ∼40 nm), which has been replicated in vitro by slow stretching of a 3-dimensional tendon-like construct containing embryonic tenocytes.
claims.source: During stage 1 there is a modest increase in fibril diameter (to ∼40 nm), which has been replicated in vitro by slow stretching of a 3-dimensional (3D) tendon-like construct containing embryonic tenocytes (Kalson et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2011.

claims.claim: At birth (in the mouse), the unimodal distribution of narrow fibrils is quickly (within a few days) replaced by a bimodal distribution of fibril diameters with a range of 35–400 nm.
claims.source: At birth (in the mouse), the unimodal distribution of narrow fibrils is quickly (within a few days) replaced by a bimodal distribution of fibril diameters with a range of 35–400 nm (Goh et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Goh et al., 2012 and data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The transition from unimodal to bimodal distributions specifies the onset of stage 2.
claims.source: The transition from unimodal to bimodal distributions specifies the onset of stage 2.
claims.evidence: This is a definition based on the observed changes in fibril diameter distributions.

claims.claim: Crimp becomes evident early in embryonic development and provides the biomechanically important 'toe-region' to the force–extension curve.
claims.source: Crimp becomes evident early in embryonic development (Shah et al., 1982) and provides the biomechanically important 'toe-region' to the force–extension curve (Shah et al., 1982).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Shah et al., 1982.

claims.claim: Mathematical modelling of crimped collagen fibrils in tendon suggests crimp to be helical in structure.
claims.source: Crimp structure has been investigated by plane polarised light microscopy and by SEM (Raspanti et al., 2005; Franchi et al., 2007), but the structure of crimp is still debated; numerous studies describe a planar 2D undulating crimp, but mathematical modelling of crimped collagen fibrils in tendon suggests crimp to be helical in structure (Grytz and Meschke, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Grytz and Meschke, 2009.

claims.claim: At E15.5 the vast majority of collagen fibrils had near-circular outlines and were therefore perpendicular (to a close approximation) to the tendon long axis.
claims.source: The results showed that at E15.5 the vast majority of collagen fibrils had near-circular outlines and were therefore perpendicular (to a close approximation) to the tendon long axis.
claims.evidence: This is based on TEM observations of transverse sections as shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: At E15.5, collagen fibrils were organised in small groups termed 'fibril bundles' that occurred in channels defined by the plasma membranes of surrounding cells.
claims.source: The fibrils were organised in small groups, which occurred in channels defined by the plasma membranes of surrounding cells. These groups of fibrils are termed 'fibril bundles' (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on TEM observations shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: At E15.5, collagen fibrils are being synthesised in fibripositors at the cell-matrix interface.
claims.source: At this stage of development the collagen fibrils are being synthesised in fibripositors at the cell-matrix interface (Kalson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2013 and observation of fibripositors in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: At birth the number of fibril profiles in fibril bundles increases >fourfold compared to E15.5.
claims.source: At birth the number of fibril profiles in fibril bundles increases >fourfold, and the fibril bundles are well defined by cellular plasma membrane extensions (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D and TEM images in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: TEM images showed electron dense cell–cell junctions between adjacent cell membrane extensions.
claims.source: TEM images showed electron dense cell–cell junctions between adjacent cell membrane extensions (Waggett et al., 2006; Richardson et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Waggett et al., 2006 and Richardson et al., 2007, and observations in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In 6 weeks postnatal tendon, fibril bundles have grown in lateral size and are separated by elongated cell processes.
claims.source: In 6 weeks postnatal tendon, fibril bundles have grown in lateral size and are separated by striking elongated cell processes (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on TEM observations shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Mean fibril diameter increased from 35.4 nm ± 0.2 nm at E15.5, to 46.5 ± 1.1 nm at birth and 160.1 ± 3.4 nm at 6 weeks postnatal.
claims.source: Analysis of TEM images demonstrated that fibril diameter increased during development, with mean fibril diameter increasing from 35.4 nm ± 0.2 nm at E15.5, to 46.5 ± 1.1 nm at birth and 160.1 ± 3.4 nm at 6 weeks postnatal (Table 1, Figure 2A,B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements presented in Table 1 and Figure 2A-C.

claims.claim: A bimodal distribution of diameters was found in 6 week postnatal tendon.
claims.source: A bimodal distribution of diameters was found in 6 week postnatal tendon, as previously described (Parry et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2C and citation to Parry et al., 1978.

claims.claim: The increase in fibril diameter occurred uniformly throughout the ECM, and was not confined to fibrils close to the cell.
claims.source: Notably, the increase in fibril diameter occurred uniformly throughout the ECM, and was not confined to fibrils close to the cell.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from TEM images that is critical to understanding the mechanism of fibril growth.

claims.claim: Approximately 700 fibrils were found in each fibril bundle at birth and also at 6 weeks postnatal.
claims.source: After birth the number of fibrils stabilised; approximately 700 fibrils were found in each fibril bundle at birth and also at 6 weeks postnatal (Figure 2D, p = >0.1, Data in Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The number of fibril bundles per nucleus was constant between newborn and 6 weeks (7.4 ± 0.3 bundles per cell vs 7.3 ± 0.3).
claims.source: At the same time as the number of fibril profiles per bundle had stabilised the number of fibril bundles per nucleus was also constant (7.4 ± 0.3 bundles per cell vs 7.3 ± 0.3 in newborn vs 6 week, p = >0.1, Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Fibripositors were absent from 6 week tail tendon.
claims.source: Fibripositors (sites of fibril formation during stage 1) were absent from 6 week tail tendon.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from TEM images of 6 week tendon.

claims.claim: The number of fibril profiles per μm2 fell by a factor of ∼10 during development as the diameter of the fibrils increased.
claims.source: The number of fibril profiles per μm2 fell by a factor of ∼10 during development as the diameter of the fibrils increased (Figure 2F)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Fibril area fraction (FAF) increased during development from 1.4 ± 0.3% at E15.5, to 17.6 ± 1.3% at newborn, to 76.4 ± 1.3% at 6 weeks.
claims.source: fibril area fraction (FAF) increased during development from 1.4 ± 0.3% at E15.5, to 17.6 ± 1.3% at newborn, to 76.4 ± 1.3% at 6 weeks (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2G and Table 1.

claims.claim: The mean fibril area increased from 1006.5 ± 13.8 nm2 at E15.5, to 2137.9 ± 370.9 nm2 at newborn to 24,606.8 ± 933.0 nm2 at 6 weeks.
claims.source: Corresponding with increase in fibril diameter, the mean fibril area increased from 1006.5 ± 13.8 nm2 at E15.5, to 2137.9 ± 370.9 nm2 at newborn to 24,606.8 ± 933.0 nm2 at 6 weeks (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2H and Table 1.

claims.claim: At E15.5, cells are rounded and close together.
claims.source: The cells at E15.5 are rounded and close together.
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Cell bodies move apart as fibril bundles increase in size, eventually becoming star shaped (in transverse section) at 6 weeks postnatal.
claims.source: The cell bodies move apart as fibril bundles increase in size, eventually becoming star shaped (in transverse section) at 6 weeks postnatal.
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Cells are stacked on top of each other, maintaining the precise longitudinal alignment of the fibril bundles.
claims.source: Longitudinal views (B and C) show the close relationship of cells, which are stacked on top of each other, thereby maintaining the precise longitudinal alignment of the fibril bundles.
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: In newborn and 6 week tendon the fibril bundles had a regular wavy configuration (crimp).
claims.source: Reconstructing the fibril bundles in three dimensions (in red in Figure 3C) showed that in newborn and 6 week tendon the fibril bundles had a regular wavy configuration (crimp).
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Cell body length decreased during development from 60 ± 2 μm at E15.5, to 55 ± 3 μm at birth, to 27 ± 2 μm at 6 weeks.
claims.source: Cell body length decreased during development from 60 ± 2 μm at E15.5, to 55 ± 3 μm at birth, to 27 ± 2 μm at 6 weeks (Data in Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM reconstructions.

claims.claim: Cell volume remains relatively constant during postnatal matrix growth between newborn and 6 weeks.
claims.source: Calculation of cell dimensions demonstrated that cell volume remains relatively constant during this period of matrix growth between newborn and 6 weeks (Figure 4D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Cell surface area increases greatly during postnatal development due to the growth of long cell processes.
claims.source: but the cell surface area increases greatly due to the growth of these long processes (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: When isolated from tendon and plated on plastic, tendon cells become flat and have the characteristic appearance of a fibroblast in culture.
claims.source: When isolated from tendon and plated on plastic the cell shape changed radically: in 2D cell culture the cells become flat and have the characteristic appearance of a fibroblast in culture (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on light microscopy observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There was no difference in the surface area of the cells when cultured on plastic comparing E15.5 cells and 6 week cells.
claims.source: There was no difference in the surface area of the cells when cultured on plastic comparing E15.5 cells and 6 week cells (Data in Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The number of cells per unit volume of tendon tissue fell significantly from 1.26 ± 0.02 to 0.91 ± 0.02 cells per 1000 µm3 between E15.5 and birth, to 0.14 ± 0.01 at 6 weeks.
claims.source: The number of cells per unit volume of tendon tissue fell significantly from 1.26 ± 0.02 to 0.91 ± 0.02 cells per 1000 µm3 between E15.5 and birth, to 0.14 ± 0.01 at 6 weeks (p = <0.05, Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM reconstructions shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Cells per unit area of transverse tendon area showed a significant fall from 30.1 ± 0.6 cells per 1000 µm2 (E.15.5) to 20.5 ± 0.8 (newborn) to 1.9 ± 0.1 (6 week).
claims.source: Measurement of cells per unit area of transverse tendon area showed a significant fall from 30.1 ± 0.6 cells per 1000 µm2 (E.15.5) to 20.5 ± 0.8 (newborn) to 1.9 ± 0.1 (6 week, p = <0.05, Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: At birth cell nuclei were spaced 39.9 ± 1.8 µm apart (on the longitudinal axis) and at 6-weeks they were 27.5 ± 1.1 µm apart.
claims.source: At birth cell nuclei were spaced 39.9 ± 1.8 µm apart (on the longitudinal axis) and at 6-weeks they were 27.5 ± 1.1 µm apart (p = <0.05, Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The discrepancy between cell length and distance between nuclei in newborn tissue was due to overlap of cells in stacks.
claims.source: The discrepancy between cell length and distance between nuclei in newborn tissue was due to overlap of cells in stacks (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from 3D reconstructions shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: There is a relative increase in the number of cells in longitudinal axis in cell channels during tendon growth comparing newborn with 6 week tendon.
claims.source: These data suggest that there is a relative increase in the number of cells in longitudinal axis in cell channels during tendon growth comparing newborn with 6 week tendon.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data on cell spacing and overlap.

claims.claim: The horizontal distance between cell nuclei increased from 6.2 ± 0.2 to 31.5 ± 0.9 µm from birth to 6 weeks.
claims.source: The horizontal distance between cell nuclei increased from 6.2 ± 0.2 to 31.5 ± 0.9 µm from birth to 6 weeks (p = <0.05, Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: At E15.5 no distinct cell membrane channels were formed via membrane protrusions contacting adjacent cells.
claims.source: At E15.5 no distinct cell membrane channels were formed via membrane protrusions contacting adjacent cells; instead groups of narrow-diameter fibrils were seen between adjacent cell membranes or enclosed in cell membrane invaginations (as shown in Figures 1A, 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, data in Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Newborn tenocytes formed protrusions that contacted adjacent cells and formed channels surrounding fibril bundles.
claims.source: Newborn tenocytes formed protrusions that contacted adjacent cells; these formed channels surrounding fibril bundles (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: At 6 weeks a similar morphology of cell–cell contact was found as in newborn, although the cell processes were much longer.
claims.source: At 6 weeks a similar morphology of cell–cell contact was found, although the cell processes were much longer (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Immunofluorescence staining revealed positive immunolocalisation of connexins 32 and 43 in mature (6 week) tendon.
claims.source: Furthermore, immunofluorescence staining against connexins 32 and 43 revealed positive immunolocalisation of cell–cell junctions in mature (6 week) tendon (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claims.claim: In newborn tendon each tendon cell forms distinct channel-defining protrusions that contact, on average, 4.6 ± 0.1 adjacent cells.
claims.source: Quantitation of cell–cell contacts showed that in newborn tendon each tendon cell forms distinct channel-defining protrusions that contact, on average, 4.6 ± 0.1 adjacent cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM reconstructions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: At 6 weeks each tendon cell contacts 4.5 ± 0.1 adjacent cells.
claims.source: At 6 weeks each tendon cell contacts 4.5 ± 0.1 adjacent cells (p = >0.05, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM reconstructions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The number of protrusions per cell that contacted adjacent cells was similar in newborn and 6 week tendon (8.2 ± 0.2 vs 8.3 ± 0.2).
claims.source: The number of protrusions per cell that contacted adjacent cells was also similar in newborn and 6 week tendon (8.2 ± 0.2 vs 8.3 ± 0.2, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM reconstructions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: At E15.5 an undulation or wavy pattern is seen in fibril bundles, but is neither regular nor well defined.
claims.source: At E15.5 an undulation or wavy pattern is seen, but is neither regular nor well defined.
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: By birth the fibril bundles have developed regular undulations, of defined and consistent wavelength.
claims.source: By birth the fibril bundles have developed regular undulations, of defined and consistent wavelength.
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The undulations in fibril bundles are in axial-register in newborn tendon.
claims.source: Importantly the undulations are in axial-register (see Figure 7B, middle panel).
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The crimp structure derives from a helical spring sub-structure, and is not simply a planar (2D) undulation.
claims.source: These data show the crimp to derive from a helical spring sub-structure, and is not simply a planar (2D) undulation.
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7C demonstrating the spiral nature of crimp.

claims.claim: The wavelength of the crimp increases during development from 14 ± 0.3 μm at birth to 99 ± 2.5 μm at 6 weeks.
claims.source: The wavelength of the crimp increases during development from 14 ± 0.3 μm at birth to 99 ± 2.5 μm at 6 weeks (Table 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Data in Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM shown in Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The crimp helix radius was 1.6 ± 0.1 μm at birth and 2.3 ± 0.1 at 6 weeks.
claims.source: The crimp helix radius (the distance from the central axis) was 1.6 ± 0.1 μm at birth and 2.3 ± 0.1 at 6 weeks.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: Tail length increased from 6.1 ± 0.3 mm (E15.5) to 10.9 ± 0.9 mm (newborn) to 67.6 ± 0.3 mm (6 week); overall a factor of 10 increase.
claims.source: Tail length increased from 6.1 ± 0.3 mm (E15.5) to 10.9 ± 0.9 mm (newborn) to 67.6 ± 0.3 mm (6 week); overall a factor of 10 increase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: The increase in tail length between newborn and 6 weeks closely matches the change in crimp wavelength (∼factor of 6–7 fold increase).
claims.source: The increase in length between newborn and 6 weeks closely matches the change in crimp wavelength (∼factor of 6–7 fold increase).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the data for tail length and crimp wavelength.

claims.claim: In 119 out of 120 specimens examined, the helical coil turns in a left-handed spiral.
claims.source: In 119 out of 120 specimens we have so far examined we have consistently found the helical coil to turn in a left-handed spiral.
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from multiple SBF-SEM reconstructions.

claims.claim: In one specimen from 6 week mouse a right-handed helix was observed.
claims.source: In one specimen from 6 week mouse we observed a right-handed helix.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation from one SBF-SEM reconstruction.

claims.claim: The alternating handedness continues from polypeptide chains (left-handed helix), to collagen molecules (right-handed), to microfibrils (left-handed) and collagen fibrils (right-handed).
claims.source: This continues the alternating handedness from polypeptide chains (left-handed helix), to collagen molecules (right-handed), to microfibrils (left-handed) and collagen fibrils (right-handed, as described in [Holmes et al., 2001]).
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge and citation to Holmes et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The fibrils in tendon bundles form a left-handed helical macrostructure.
claims.source: These data show that the fibrils in tendon bundles then form a left-handed helical macrostructure.
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The left-handed spiral structure of fibril bundles has been observed in all anatomically distinct tendons examined using SBF-SEM, including mouse Achilles tendon and chick metatarsal tendons.
claims.source: We have observed this left-handed spiral structure of fibril bundles in all the anatomically distinct tendons we have examined using SBF-SEM, including mouse Achilles tendon and chick metatarsal tendons, with different biomechanical properties compared with mouse-tail tendon, an axial tendon (Benjamin et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from multiple SBF-SEM studies and citation to Benjamin et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Mean fibril length increased significantly from 125 ± 18 µm at E15.5, to 578 ± 17 µm in newborn tendon.
claims.source: This demonstrated a significant increase in fibril length through development, from 125 ± 18 µm at E15.5, to 578 ± 17 µm in newborn tendon (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, p = <0.05, Data in Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fibril tracking data from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: At E15.5, 160 fibril tips were identified within 10,000 µm fibril lengths tracked.
claims.source: At E15.5 160 fibril tips were identified (within 10,000 µm fibril lengths tracked).
claims.evidence: This is based on fibril tracking from SBF-SEM data.

claims.claim: In newborn mouse tendon, 69 tips were found over ∼20,000 µm fibril lengths tracked.
claims.source: In newborn mouse tendon, 69 tips were found (over ∼20,000 µm fibril lengths tracked).
claims.evidence: This is based on fibril tracking from SBF-SEM data.

claims.claim: At 6 weeks, 16 tips were identified within 10,000 µm fibril lengths tracked, all occurring in fibrils less than 150 nm in diameter.
claims.source: At 6 weeks fibril tips were rare; 16 tips were identified within 10,000 µm fibril lengths tracked, all occurring in fibrils less than 150 nm in diameter (the smaller population of postnatal fibrils).
claims.evidence: This is based on fibril tracking from SBF-SEM data.

claims.claim: No fibril tips were found in fibrils >150 nm in diameter at 6 weeks.
claims.source: No tips were found in fibrils >150 nm in diameter.
claims.evidence: This is based on fibril tracking from SBF-SEM data.

claims.claim: The estimated mean-length of fibrils less than 150 nm diameter at 6 weeks is 1250 ± 305 µm.
claims.source: This gave an estimate of mean-length of 1250 ± 305 µm for fibrils less than 150 nm diameter.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from fibril tracking data from SBF-SEM.

claims.claim: Tendon development occurs in a two-stage process.
claims.source: In conclusion, we have shown that tendon development occurs in a two-stage process.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: In stage 1 the organisation of fibroblasts and the cellular channels for fibril deposition and growth are established, and cell-mediated control of collagen fibril deposition occurs.
claims.source: In stage 1 the organisation of fibroblasts and the cellular channels for fibril deposition and growth are established, and cell-mediated control of collagen fibril deposition occurs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing fibril formation in fibripositors and establishment of cell-cell contacts during embryonic development.

claims.claim: Stage 1 sets the developmental template for structure-based matrix expansion of the existing matrix in stage 2.
claims.source: This sets the developmental template for structure-based matrix expansion of the existing matrix in stage 2, which drives the increase in the size of the matrix that underpins tissue growth.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that fibril numbers remain constant postnatally while fibrils grow in diameter and length.

claims.claim: The cell-regulated number of cell processes define the boundaries of collagen fibril bundles and help to maintain the tramline organization of cells in the mature tissue.
claims.source: Important features include the cell-regulated number of cell processes that define the boundaries of collagen fibril bundles and help to maintain the tramline organization of cells in the mature tissue.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing stable numbers of cell-cell contacts and fibril bundles per cell during postnatal development.

claims.claim: These mechanisms could be a paradigm for the growth of other matrix-rich tissues that are abundant in collagen fibrils.
claims.source: These mechanisms could be a paradigm for the growth of other matrix-rich tissues that are abundant in collagen fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claims.claim: The close association of cells with bundles suggests that the cell shape strongly influences the configuration of the crimp structure.
claims.source: The close association of cells with bundles suggests that the cell shape strongly influences the configuration of the crimp structure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed close relationship between cell shape and fibril bundle crimp shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claims.claim: Cell force generated by the actin-myosin system can create a crimp structure.
claims.source: This is consistent with studies suggesting that cell force generated by the actin-myosin system can create a crimp structure (Herchenhan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Herchenhan et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The length increase of the mouse-tail from newborn to 6 weeks by a factor of ∼6.2× closely matches the increase in crimp wavelength of ∼7.1×.
claims.source: The length increase of the mouse-tail from newborn to 6 weeks by a factor of ∼6.2× closely matches the increase in crimp wavelength of ∼7.1×.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of tail length and crimp wavelength measurements from Table 1.

claims.claim: The close match between tail length increase and crimp wavelength increase suggests a simple crimp elongation process in synchrony with bundle and tissue elongation.
claims.source: This suggests a simple crimp elongation process in synchrony with bundle and tissue elongation.

results.result: Collagen fibril number increases during embryonic development (E15.5 to birth) and then remains constant during postnatal growth (birth to 6 weeks), with approximately 700 fibrils per bundle at birth and 6 weeks. Embryonic growth is driven by increases in fibril number and length, while postnatal growth is driven by increases in fibril diameter and length.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C34, C40, C41, and C100 provide converging quantitative evidence from TEM and SBF-SEM showing fibril numbers increase >4-fold from E15.5 to birth (C34), then stabilize at ~700 fibrils per bundle (C40, p>0.1). Claims C3 and C4 correctly interpret these data in the context of developmental mechanisms. The statistical analysis and multiple imaging modalities provide strong support.

results.result: Fibril diameter increases significantly during development (35.4±0.2 nm at E15.5 to 46.5±1.1 nm at birth to 160.1±3.4 nm at 6 weeks), with a transition from unimodal to bimodal diameter distribution marking the onset of stage 2 development. This is accompanied by increases in fibril area fraction (1.4% to 76.4%) and mean fibril area.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C44, and C45 provide quantitative measurements from TEM with clear statistical support (Table 1, Figure 2). Claims C21, C27, C28, and C38 correctly identify the unimodal-to-bimodal transition as defining developmental stages. The uniform increase in diameter throughout the ECM (C39) is a critical observation supporting the proposed growth mechanism.

results.result: Tendon exhibits a helical crimp structure that is established during embryogenesis and persists postnatally. The crimp is irregular at E15.5, becomes regular and in axial-register by birth, and derives from a left-handed helical spring sub-structure (observed in 119/120 specimens). Crimp wavelength increases from 14±0.3 μm at birth to 99±2.5 μm at 6 weeks.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C68-C73, C76, and C79 are supported by 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM (Figure 7) showing the helical nature of crimp. The quantitative measurements of wavelength and helix radius (Table 1) are well-documented. The observation of left-handed helicity in 119/120 specimens (C76) provides strong statistical support. This resolves prior debate about crimp structure (C30, C118).

results.result: Fibril diameter increases uniformly throughout the ECM independent of distance from cells, and the data do not support shaft-to-shaft fibril fusion as a major mechanism. Instead, fibril growth appears to be interface-controlled (structure-based) rather than diffusion-limited, consistent with the surface-nucleation-and-propagation (SNP) model.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 provides the critical observation that fibril diameter is uniform throughout ECM. Claims C99, C101, and C102 provide evidence against fusion (few fusion events observed, no irregular fibrils, constant fibril numbers). Claims C105, C109, and C110 logically infer interface-controlled growth from these observations. The reasoning is sound and supported by the data, though the SNP model itself is cited from prior work (C103-C106).

results.result: Mean fibril length increases significantly during development from 125±18 μm at E15.5 to 578±17 μm at birth. At 6 weeks, fibril tips are rare in large-diameter fibrils (>150 nm), with estimated mean length of 1250±305 μm for smaller fibrils (<150 nm).
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 are supported by fibril tracking data from SBF-SEM (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). The methodology of counting fibril tips over tracked lengths is appropriate. However, the inability to estimate length for large-diameter fibrils at 6 weeks (C85, C86) is a limitation. The statistical significance (p<0.05) for E15.5 to newborn comparison strengthens the result.

results.result: Cell morphology changes dramatically during development. At E15.5 cells are rounded and close together (60±2 μm length). By 6 weeks, cells are star-shaped in cross-section with prominent lateral extensions (27±2 μm body length), stacked longitudinally. Cell volume remains constant during postnatal growth, but surface area increases greatly due to long cellular processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48, C50-C52, and C111-C113 are supported by 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM (Figures 3, 4). Quantitative measurements of cell dimensions (Figure 4D, E) show constant volume but increased surface area. The observations are internally consistent and well-documented with both qualitative (reconstructions) and quantitative (measurements) evidence.

results.result: Cell density decreases significantly during development (1.26±0.02 to 0.14±0.01 cells per 1000 μm³ from E15.5 to 6 weeks). Longitudinal spacing between nuclei decreases from 39.9±1.8 μm at birth to 27.5±1.1 μm at 6 weeks due to cell overlap, while transverse spacing increases from 6.2±0.2 to 31.5±0.9 μm.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 provide quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM reconstructions (Figure 5) with statistical significance (p<0.05). The explanation of cell overlap (C58) is supported by 3D reconstructions (Figure 5A). The inference about relative increase in longitudinal cell number (C59) follows logically from the spacing data. The measurements are internally consistent.

results.result: Cell-cell contacts evolve during development. At E15.5, distinct membrane channels are absent. By birth, cells form protrusions contacting 4.6±0.1 adjacent cells with 8.2±0.2 protrusions per cell. These numbers remain constant at 6 weeks (4.5±0.1 cells, 8.3±0.2 protrusions), though processes are longer. Connexins 32 and 43 are present in mature tendon.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63, C65-C67 are supported by SBF-SEM reconstructions (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) with quantitative analysis showing no significant difference between newborn and 6 weeks (p>0.05). Claim C64 provides immunofluorescence evidence for gap junction proteins. The stability of cell-cell contact numbers during postnatal growth is a key finding supporting the proposed model.

results.result: The authors propose a two-stage model of tendon development: Stage 1 (embryonic) establishes fibroblast organization, cellular channels, and fibril number/position, which then serves as a template for Stage 2 (postnatal) structure-based matrix expansion through fibril diameter and length increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, and C87-C90 represent the central interpretive model. This model is well-supported by the collective data showing: (1) fibril numbers stabilize at birth (C2, C40-C41), (2) cell-cell contacts stabilize (C65-C67), (3) postnatal growth occurs via diameter/length increases (C4, C37), and (4) uniform diameter growth throughout ECM (C39). The model logically integrates multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Tail length increases 10-fold during development (6.1±0.3 mm at E15.5 to 67.6±0.3 mm at 6 weeks). The 6.2-fold increase from newborn to 6 weeks closely matches the 7.1-fold increase in crimp wavelength, suggesting crimp elongation occurs in synchrony with tissue elongation.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 and C94-C95 provide measurements (Table 1) and make a logical inference about the relationship between tissue length and crimp wavelength. The close correspondence (6.2× vs 7.1×) supports the inference of synchronized elongation (C95). This is a reasonable interpretation of the quantitative data, though the mechanism of synchronization is not directly tested.

results.result: At E15.5, collagen fibrils are perpendicular to the tendon long axis, organized in small bundles within channels defined by cell membranes, and are synthesized in fibripositors at the cell-matrix interface. Fibripositors are absent from 6-week tendon.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by TEM observations (Figure 1A) and citation to prior work on fibripositors (C33, Kalson et al., 2013). Claim C42 notes the absence of fibripositors at 6 weeks. These observations are consistent with the two-stage model and the transition from active fibril synthesis (stage 1) to matrix expansion (stage 2).

results.result: When isolated from tendon and cultured on plastic, cells from both E15.5 and 6 weeks adopt a flat fibroblast morphology with similar surface area, contrasting with their distinct 3D morphologies in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by light microscopy observations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing no significant difference in 2D culture surface area. This demonstrates that the dramatic differences in cell morphology observed in vivo (C46-C47, C111-C112) are dependent on the 3D tissue environment, not intrinsic differences in cell properties.

results.result: The left-handed helical crimp structure continues the pattern of alternating handedness from molecular to supramolecular levels (polypeptide→molecule→microfibril→fibril→bundle). This structure has been observed in all anatomically distinct tendons examined, including mouse Achilles and chick metatarsal tendons.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is supported by citation to established knowledge (Holmes et al., 2001) about molecular handedness. Claim C80 extends the current findings to other tendon types, supported by the authors' SBF-SEM observations and citation to Benjamin et al., 2008. This suggests the helical crimp is a general feature of tendon structure, not specific to mouse tail tendon.

results.result: The close association between cells and fibril bundles suggests cell shape influences crimp configuration. Cell bodies move laterally apart due to ECM expansion while maintaining longitudinal relationships, generating the tramline organization of mature tendon. This is consistent with cell force generation by the actin-myosin system.
results.evaluation: Claims C92 and C114 are inferences supported by the observed close cell-bundle relationship (Figures 3, 7) and cell spacing data (C60). Claim C93 cites prior work (Herchenhan et al., 2012) suggesting a mechanism. While the inferences are reasonable and consistent with the data, direct evidence for cell force generation in crimp formation is not provided in this study.

results.result: The authors preserved tendon tension during fixation by fixing whole tails without disturbing axial attachment to skeleton. They observed no kinks in crimp structure (as previously reported by Raspanti et al., 2005), but instead found a left-handed spiral.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 describes the methodological approach to preserve native crimp structure, citing Shah et al., 1977. Claim C118 contrasts current findings with prior reports. The 3D reconstructions (Figure 7) support the spiral structure. The discrepancy with prior work may reflect differences in sample preparation or imaging methods (SBF-SEM vs. SEM after chemical treatment).

results.result: Background claims about tendon function and development: tendons transmit large tensile forces (~16 kN/kg body mass) via aligned collagen fibrils; embryonic growth occurs by cell number increase; functional tendon development begins with collagen fibril appearance in the ECM.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C1, and C20 represent established knowledge in the field, supported by citations (C8-C9: Harrison et al., 2010) or general acceptance. These provide context for the study but are not novel findings. They are appropriately cited and accurately stated.

results.result: Background on tendon development molecular biology: Scleraxis, tenomodulin, Mohawk, EGR1/2 are transcription factors involved in tendon development; TGFβ and FGF are key signaling pathways; collagen types I, III, V, XII, XIV and proteoglycans are ECM components.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C19 summarize prior work on molecular aspects of tendon development, all supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context but are not findings of the current study. The authors correctly note that molecular markers alone do not explain structural development (implied in introduction).

results.result: Background on tendon developmental stages and structure: Two stages distinguished by fibril diameter distribution; stage 1 begins at E12.5 with narrow fibrils in fibripositors; stage 2 marked by bimodal distribution; fibril bundles undergo rotation; crimp provides toe-region in force-extension curves.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C30 summarize prior knowledge about tendon development stages and structure, supported by multiple citations. These establish the framework for the current study's findings. The authors build on this foundation with their 3D structural analysis.

results.result: Background on fibril growth mechanisms: Fibril fusion is regulated by collagen molecule directionality, unipolar fibril tips, and proteoglycans; fusion reduces fibril numbers but not volume fraction. The SNP model proposes structure-based growth via molecular accretion at specific binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 and C103-C104, C106 describe established models of fibril growth from prior literature (Kadler et al., 1990; Graham et al., 2000; Birk et al., 1995; Holmes et al., 1992, 1998; Trotter et al., 1998, 2000). These provide theoretical context for interpreting the current findings. The authors use these models to explain their observations.

results.result: The proposed mechanisms could be a paradigm for growth of other matrix-rich collagen-containing tissues.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is speculative about broader implications. While the observation of similar helical crimp in other tendons (C80) provides some support, extension to other collagen-rich tissues (e.g., ligaments, dermis, cornea) requires additional investigation. The claim is appropriately tentative ('could be') but lacks direct supporting evidence.

results.result: Theoretical predictions about fibril growth: If growth were non-specific and uncoordinated, axial mass profiles would show random fluctuations; if diffusion-limited, fibrils closer to cells would be larger.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are logical inferences about what would be expected under alternative growth mechanisms. These serve as null hypotheses that are rejected based on the observation of uniform diameter distribution (C39) and structured growth. The reasoning is sound and helps support the interface-controlled growth model.

results.result: Crimp appears early in embryonic development but the mechanism of crimp formation remains unknown.
results.evaluation: Claim C115 is supported by citation (Shah et al., 1982). Claim C116 accurately describes the state of knowledge prior to this study. The current work provides new structural information about crimp (helical nature) but does not fully elucidate the formation mechanism, though it suggests cell shape influence (C92).

results.result: Fibril bundles are continuous over measured distances, forming parallel spirals in axial register to provide uniform biomechanical properties when loaded, with close cell-bundle relationship.
results.evaluation: Claim C119 integrates observations from 3D reconstructions (Figure 7) about bundle continuity, spiral organization, and axial registration. The inference about uniform biomechanical properties is reasonable given the structural organization, though not directly tested. The claim appropriately qualifies the observation to 'distances measured' acknowledging limitations.
